Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MARTINSBURG, West Virginia (CNN) -- Hardly a day that goes by that you won't find Tracey Wygal working out at the gym. Tracey Wygal weighed 295 pounds before starting a "clean diet," keeping a food journal and exercising. The 30-year-old middle-school teacher does cardio exercise, strength trains and follows what she calls a "clean diet." That's quite a change for a woman who tipped the scales eight years ago at 295 pounds. Wygal first started gaining weight in her early teens. A fast-food diet and little to no exercise helped her pack on the pounds, and her weight ballooned to over 200 pounds. "It was my first year out of college, and that number, along with being diagnosed as morbidly obese, was very frightening," remembers Wygal. "I went to several doctors, trying to get them to prescribe a weight-loss pill." But none of her doctors would give her the quick fix she was looking for. Instead, a physician handed her a 1,600-calorie-a-day diet and told her to start moving. At first, Wygal was shocked and refused to begin a diet that she thought was too restrictive. Even though her weight was rapidly approaching 300 pounds, she believed she had a pretty good diet and an active lifestyle. As her weight crept up, Wygal grew more frustrated, and eventually she decided it was time to gain control of her life. She started by keeping track of her daily calorie intake in a food diary and soon realized that her eating was worse than she thought.  Watch more from Tracey Wygal on her weight loss success. » . "I was amazed by how many calories I was eating," Wygal said. "The food diary showed me that I really needed to get my food intake under control and helped me maintain my diet realistically." She also started exercising. At first, Wygal says, she was too embarrassed to go to a gym, so she bought an elliptical machine and started working out 15 minutes a day in her apartment. "It was all I could do at first. I didn't give up, though," she said. "Gradually, my endurance improved. After losing about 30 pounds, I decided to join a small gym." Several months later, Wygal was ready to take the next step. She hired a trainer and began a short strength-training program. That's when something clicked. Instead of feeling intimidated, Wygal started to love her workouts and the physical changes taking shape with her body. Ready to take the next step, she joined a larger gym, began researching different workouts and got into weight training. Over the next three years, she lost 120 pounds and dropped seven dress sizes. Wygal, who's 5 feet 10 inches tall, says the fear of gaining weight motivates her to stick to her diet and exercise regimen because she never wants to look like she did at 295 pounds. Now comfortable with her weight, which she says fluctuates between 170 and 180 pounds, Wygal works out at least five to six days a week. She says the key to losing weight and keeping it off is being honest about what you eat, writing it down and staying consistent. She wants people to know they can do it, but there are no quick fixes or easy outs -- just hard work. "It won't happen overnight," Wygal advises. "Know that it will take time but it is worth it in the end." iReport.com: Have you lost weight? Send your story, photos and video . CNN Medical News producer Matt Sloane contributed to this report.

Today, the 30-year-old middle-school teacher does cardio, strength trains and follows her clean-eating plan—a remarkable change for a woman who tipped the scales at 295 pounds eight years ago.

Wygal began gaining weight in her early teens. A fast-food diet and little to no exercise caused her to pack on the pounds, and her weight eventually climbed above 200 pounds.

“It was my first year out of college, and that number, along with being diagnosed as morbidly obese, was very frightening,” Wygal remembers. “I went to several doctors, trying to get them to prescribe a weight-loss pill.”

None of her doctors, however, would give her the quick fix she wanted. Instead, one physician gave her a 1,600-calorie-per-day diet and told her to start moving.

At first, Wygal was shocked and refused to begin a diet she considered too restrictive. Even as her weight rapidly approached 300 pounds, she believed she had a fairly healthy diet and an active lifestyle.

As her weight continued to rise, Wygal became increasingly frustrated. Eventually, she decided it was time to take control of her life. She began recording her daily calorie intake in a food diary and soon realized that her eating habits were worse than she had thought.

“I was amazed by how many calories I was eating,” Wygal said. “The food diary showed me that I really needed to get my food intake under control and helped me maintain my diet realistically.”

“It was all I could do at first. I didn’t give up, though,” she said. “Gradually, my endurance improved. After losing about 30 pounds, I decided to join a small gym.”

Several months later, Wygal was ready to take the next step. She hired a trainer and began a short strength-training program. That was when something clicked. Rather than feeling intimidated, she began to love her workouts and the physical changes taking shape in her body.

Ready to progress further, Wygal joined a larger gym, began researching different workouts and took up weight training. Over the next three years, she lost 120 pounds and dropped seven dress sizes.

Wygal, who is 5 feet 10 inches tall, says the fear of regaining the weight motivates her to remain committed to her diet and exercise regimen because she never wants to look as she did at 295 pounds.

Now comfortable with her weight, which she says fluctuates between 170 and 180 pounds, Wygal works out at least five or six days a week. She says the key to losing weight and keeping it off is to be honest about what you eat, write it down and remain consistent.

“It won’t happen overnight,” Wygal advises. “Know that it will take time, but it is worth it in the end.”

MARTINSBURG, West Virginia (CNN) — Tracey Wygal can be found at the gym nearly every day.

The 30-year-old middle-school teacher combines cardiovascular workouts and strength training with an eating plan she describes as a “clean diet.” She also records what she eats. Her current routine is a dramatic departure from eight years ago, when she weighed 295 pounds.

Wygal began putting on weight during her early teenage years. Frequent fast food and almost no physical activity eventually pushed her weight above 200 pounds.

“It was my first year out of college, and that number, along with being diagnosed as morbidly obese, was very frightening,” Wygal recalls. Hoping for an immediate solution, she visited several physicians and asked them to prescribe weight-loss medication.

The doctors declined. One instead gave her a plan limiting her to 1,600 calories per day and advised her to become more physically active. Wygal initially rejected the idea because she considered the diet overly restrictive. Although she was quickly nearing 300 pounds, she still thought she ate reasonably well and led an active life.

As the number on the scale continued to rise, her frustration increased. Eventually, she resolved to take charge of her health. Her first step was documenting her daily calories in a food journal. The record soon revealed that her eating habits were far less healthy than she had believed.

Watch more about Tracey Wygal’s successful weight loss. »

“I was amazed by how many calories I was eating,” she says. According to Wygal, the journal made clear that she needed to control her food consumption and gave her a practical way to remain on track.

She began exercising as well. Initially, she felt too self-conscious to visit a gym, so she purchased an elliptical machine and used it for 15 minutes each day in her apartment.

“It was all I could do at first. I didn’t give up, though,” she says. Her stamina slowly increased, and after shedding roughly 30 pounds, she joined a small gym.

A few months afterward, Wygal progressed further by hiring a trainer and starting a brief strength-training routine. That proved to be a turning point. Her feelings of intimidation faded, and she began enjoying both the exercise and the visible changes in her body.

She later moved to a bigger gym, researched a variety of exercise routines and became involved in weight training. During the following three years, she lost 120 pounds and went down seven dress sizes.

At 5 feet 10 inches tall, Wygal now weighs between 170 and 180 pounds and feels comfortable at that size. She exercises at least five or six days each week. She says the possibility of regaining the weight keeps her committed to her nutrition and fitness program because she never wants to return to how she looked at 295 pounds.

In Wygal’s view, long-term weight loss depends on honestly acknowledging what you eat, recording it and remaining consistent. She wants others to understand that success is possible, but it requires sustained effort rather than shortcuts or instant solutions.

“It won’t happen overnight,” she advises. “Know that it will take time, but it is worth it in the end.”

CNN Medical News producer Matt Sloane contributed to this report.

# Martinsburg, West Virginia

Martinsburg, West Virginia, is a historic city in the state’s Eastern Panhandle and the county seat of Berkeley County. Conveniently located near Interstate 81, it offers easy access to Washington, D.C., Baltimore, and Northern Virginia while maintaining the welcoming atmosphere of a smaller Appalachian community.

Founded in 1778, Martinsburg has deep ties to American transportation and industrial history. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad played an important role in the city’s development, and this heritage is preserved at the Martinsburg Roundhouse, a notable historic landmark. Visitors can also explore local museums, historic homes, and architecture that reflect the city’s past.

Today, Martinsburg combines history with modern growth. Its downtown features locally owned restaurants, shops, community events, and cultural attractions. The surrounding region provides opportunities for hiking, fishing, and scenic drives, while nearby orchards and farms highlight the agricultural traditions of West Virginia’s Eastern Panhandle.

With its strategic location, rich heritage, and strong sense of community, Martinsburg is an appealing destination for visitors, families, and businesses. It serves as a gateway to the natural beauty and historic character of West Virginia.

For Tracey Wygal, change didn’t come from a crash diet or a single dramatic workout. It came from paying attention to the choices she made each day.

The 30-year-old West Virginia teacher lost 120 pounds through a combination of calorie tracking, clean eating, cardio and strength training — an approach built on consistency rather than quick fixes.

Tracking calories helped Wygal better understand portion sizes and how everyday foods fit into her goals. She also focused on minimally processed, nutrient-dense meals, while allowing her routine to become sustainable over time.

Exercise was another key part of her transformation. Cardio helped improve her endurance and increase her activity level, while strength training allowed her to build muscle and become stronger. Together, the two forms of exercise offered balance and kept her fitness routine from relying on just one strategy.

Her experience also reflects a lesson familiar to many teachers: Progress often happens gradually. Results can take time, and setbacks do not have to erase the work that came before them.

Losing 120 pounds required Wygal to repeatedly choose habits that supported her health, even when motivation may have fluctuated. By keeping track of her food, choosing cleaner options and showing up for workouts, she turned individual decisions into a new way of life.

Weight-loss needs vary, and health professionals recommend consulting a doctor or registered dietitian before making major changes to diet or exercise. But Wygal’s journey offers a straightforward message: Lasting transformation can begin with small steps, repeated day after day.

# Inspirational Health Report: Building Sustainable Habits

## Overview

A 5-foot-10 woman successfully maintained her weight between 170 and 180 pounds by focusing on steady, practical habits rather than quick fixes. Her experience demonstrates that long-term progress often comes from self-awareness, gradual change, professional support, and consistency.

## Keeping a Food Diary

Recording meals and snacks helped her become more mindful of what, when, and why she ate. The diary was not used to judge every choice; instead, it revealed patterns such as portion sizes, skipped meals, emotional eating, and foods that supported her energy.

This awareness allowed her to make manageable adjustments while still enjoying flexibility. Over time, informed choices became easier and more natural.

## Gradually Increasing Exercise

Rather than beginning with an exhausting routine, she increased her activity step by step. She started at a level that felt realistic and slowly added more walking, strength training, or workout time as her fitness improved.

This gradual approach reduced the risk of burnout and helped exercise become a regular part of her life. Each small improvement built confidence and momentum.

## Hiring a Trainer

A qualified trainer provided structure, accountability, and guidance. The trainer helped her use proper technique, choose appropriate exercises, and progress safely. Personalized workouts also made her time more effective and gave her clear goals to work toward.

Just as importantly, the trainer offered encouragement during periods when motivation was lower.

## Remaining Consistent

Consistency was the foundation of her success. She did not expect perfection and understood that occasional indulgences, missed workouts, and normal weight fluctuations were part of life. Instead of giving up after a difficult day, she returned to her routine at the next opportunity.

By repeating helpful behaviors over months and years, she maintained a stable 170-to-180-pound range without relying on extreme restrictions.

## Key Lessons

- Awareness can be more sustainable than rigid dieting.
- Gradual progress is still meaningful progress.
- Professional support can improve safety and accountability.
- A weight range allows for normal fluctuations.
- Consistency matters more than perfection.

## Conclusion

Her story shows that maintaining weight is not about one dramatic transformation. It is about building a lifestyle that can be continued. Through food journaling, progressive exercise, expert support, and a commitment to returning to healthy habits, she created a sustainable routine that supported both stability and confidence.

Health is broader than a number on the scale, so individual nutrition, fitness, and medical needs should be discussed with qualified healthcare professionals.
